_comment: Dispatch policy for scripts/hermes-cc.sh. This file used to be an INVENTORY — one entry
per repo, absence a denial. It is now a POLICY: repos are discovered under `root`, and
this file only records the exceptions. The reason is drift. The inventory listed 22 repos
while 30 sat on disk; three of them (king-smith-walkingpad-mac, linewatch, vibe-stack)
had been unreachable for as long as they had existed, and nobody noticed, because a
missing entry and a deliberate denial looked identical from the outside. A list that must
be edited every time a repo is cloned is a list that is wrong most of the time.
WHAT REPLACED 'ABSENCE IS A DENIAL'. A dispatch still names a repo and never a path —
that property is unchanged and is the one that matters, because it is what keeps a
composed path out of the interface. What changed is the answer for a name nobody has
ruled on: it is now `defaultTier` instead of a refusal. Three guards make that safe:
1. `deny` below is checked FIRST and is absolute — no tier, no override, no discovery.
2. Discovery is confined to `root`. The name must be a single path segment ('.', '..'
and dotted names are rejected), and the resolved checkout's parent must BE the
resolved root — so neither a traversal nor a symlink can point outside it.
3. It must be a real git checkout. There is no path to a repo that is not one.
`root` is ~/SourceRoot, which holds only Johannes's own repos. ~/IuRoot is work and is
not reachable from here at any tier — it is not `root` and there is no second root.
WHY `implement` IS THE DEFAULT. The tiers are not equally consequential:
investigate  read-only. Cannot lose anything.
author       + files one GitHub issue. A wrong issue is closed in two seconds.
implement    + an isolated worktree, a dispatch/… branch and a DRAFT pull request.
Never a push to a default branch, never a CI workflow. Landing it is a
separate verb (`merge`) with its own re-checks and its own daily ceiling.
The default was `author` for about a day, with `implement` on a four-repo allowlist. That
allowlist is gone (owner decision, 2026-08-02) and the reason is the same one that killed
the inventory above: a list that has to be edited before the tool can do its job is a list
that will be out of date at the moment it is needed, and the maintenance buys less than it
costs. The point of this bridge is a system that heals itself; a default that stops short
of proposing the fix makes it a system that files tickets.
KNOW WHAT THAT REACHES. `argo`, `audio-gateway` and `research-gateway` deploy to the VPS
on every push to master (GitHub Actions -> RollHook). They are now `implement`-reachable
like everything else, so the full chain is: a Slack message -> a dispatched episode -> a
draft PR -> `merge` -> production. `merge` needs `--why` AND `--confirm`, which in Slack
means Hermes had to ask and be answered first — that is the gate, and it is the same
instruction-level gate `implement` has, not a structural one. Stated here because it is
the thing a future reader should weigh if they are tempted to widen this further, and
because 'nothing here can reach production' would be a comfortable and false summary.
What actually bounds `implement` is not this file. It is the shape of the tier: an
isolated worktree, a `dispatch/…` branch, a DRAFT pull request, and `--why` AND `--confirm`
on every invocation. Nothing reaches a default branch without the `merge` verb, which
re-checks every bound against the current head, refuses any repo listed in
dotfiles/config/pr-required-repos.json, and has its own tighter ceiling of 3/day. The
worst unattended outcome here is a draft PR nobody wanted, which costs one click.
Most of these repos are public, so an issue or a draft PR is world-readable and permanent.
Also a considered, accepted cost: both are cheap to delete, and triage that finds a real
defect should be able to record — or propose — the fix without a human relaying it by hand.
The handler-side secret scan still refuses — never redacts — a brief carrying credentials,
and the skill instructs the agent to summarize rather than quote.
THE ONE EXCEPTION BELOW. The question is not 'could an episode damage this repo' — it
cannot, since nothing merges without `merge` — but 'what does this repo control if a bad
change ever did land'.
investigate  dotfiles, vps, homelab. These are the machine's own control plane:
dotfiles carries the secrets tooling and the rules that bound every agent
on this box (including this one), and vps/homelab are deployment surfaces
watched by rollhook. Read-only here is a deliberate floor, not an oversight —
it is the one place where the cost of a bad proposal is not one click.
DENIED, and staying denied:
dotfiles-private, homelab-private — private by construction. Their whole point is
that their contents are not referenced from anywhere else; an agent-readable
episode inside them would undo that.
brain — the personal vault. Read-only would be technically safe, but journal and
personal notes are not triage material, and the obsidian skill already owns that
door with conventions this tool does not implement.
A name in `deny` that also appears in `tiers` is a contradiction, not a precedence
question — hermes-cc.sh refuses to run rather than pick a winner.
